headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - the Lyme disease paper and the Long COVID paper - each built from a single uploaded document, so it describes only these two papers and not either condition in general.

The Lyme disease paper reports direct medical and out-of-pocket cost figures in 2019 euros, while the Long COVID paper reports lost-labor/productivity cost figures in 2022 US dollars, so the dollar amounts in the two papers cannot be read as equivalent or combined.

Both papers present their headline cost figures as single pooled national totals with no demographic subgroup breakdown, and each flags a different systemic gap - a diagnostic-coding gap for Lyme disease and a lack of effective treatment for Long COVID.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 24.5% of direct medical cost is not reimbursed by insurance, with patients paying 43.9 EUR (2019) out of pocket for early-stage (EM) Lyme disease and 286 EUR (2019) for disseminated/late Lyme disease, plus 190 EUR (2019) in travel costs for disseminated/late patients.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report any out-of-pocket or direct medical cost figures; it states that direct medical and non-medical costs were not quantified in the document itself.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper in this sample gives patient-paid cost figures, so financial exposure cannot be compared across the two papers on this dimension.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that productivity losses make up 46.4% of total Lyme borreliosis cost (2019 EUR) but does not give a per-person lost-labor dollar figure comparable to the Long COVID paper's method.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a mean lost-labor cost gap of 1242.04 USD/person/year (2022) for Long COVID versus never having had COVID-19, and a national 2022 lost-labor cost of 12784168675.2 USD attributable to Long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers measure work-loss burden with different methods, currencies, and years, so the scale of productivity loss cannot be read as directly comparable.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that per-patient cost for disseminated/late Lyme disease (5148 EUR, 2019) is about 26.67 times the per-patient cost for early-stage EM (193 EUR, 2019), linking later-stage diagnosis to markedly higher per-patient cost.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report a diagnostic-delay or disease-stage cost comparison; it only distinguishes acute COVID-19 without Long COVID from Long COVID (symptoms lasting 3+ months) using self-report.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper in this sample ties diagnostic stage or delay to a quantified cost escalation.

comparison_rows.dimension: Access barriers (insurance reimbursement / paid sick leave)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 75.5% of direct medical costs were reimbursed by health insurance, describing an insurance cost-sharing structure, but does not address employment leave policy.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports 81.2% paid sick leave prevalence overall versus 79.6% among those with Long COVID (a 1.6 percentage point gap) and notes the paid-sick-leave/Long COVID association did not reach statistical significance (odds ratio 0.9).

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Each paper examines a different access barrier - insurance reimbursement versus paid sick leave - so the two findings cannot be treated as measuring the same thing.

comparison_rows.dimension: How each condition's cost estimate is affected by official or survey data

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states there is no specific ICD-10-CM code for early-stage (EM) or post-treatment Lyme disease, so all hospital costs were allocated to the broader disseminated/late Lyme disease category and coding quality could not be checked, meaning claims-based hospital cost figures produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper relies on self-reported COVID-19/Long COVID history and self-reported missed workdays rather than official claims data, and flags this reliance on self-report as a limitation rather than an official-data undercount.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers describe different mechanisms by which their data may miss or misclassify cases, so neither pattern should be read as confirming the other.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states it did not collect cost data beyond 6-12 months post-diagnosis, excluded pediatric costs, and based post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome cost estimates on very small samples (6 and 3 patients).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states it has no data on direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, caregiving time, diagnostic delay, or multi-year projections, offering only a single 2022 calendar-year snapshot of missed-workday costs.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave substantial parts of total economic burden unmeasured, so neither figure should be read as a comprehensive cost-of-illness estimate.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper presents its national total and per-patient costs as single pooled figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper presents its population-level and per-person cost figures as single pooled national figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers cannot use either paper to see how economic burden differs across demographic subgroups within each condition.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper flags that Belgium's ICD-10-CM hospital coding has no dedicated code for early-stage (EM) or post-treatment Lyme disease, forcing allocation of hospital costs to a broader diagnostic category.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper flags that there are currently no effective treatments for Long COVID, leaving vaccination as the best available prevention strategy.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The systemic gaps identified are of different kinds - a data-coding gap versus a treatment gap - pointing toward different policy responses.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers present their headline cost figures as single pooled national totals without any breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.

evidence.note: The national total (5590000 EUR/year, 2019) and per-patient means (193 EUR for EM, 5148 EUR for disseminated/late Lyme disease) are reported as pooled figures with no subgroup breakdown.
The population-level estimate (12784168675.2 USD, 2022) and per-group mean costs are reported as pooled national figures with no subgroup breakdown.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers explicitly state that important cost components are missing from their burden estimate.

evidence.note: The paper states it excluded costs beyond 6-12 months post-diagnosis, pediatric costs, and most non-reimbursed hospital supplements.
The paper states it has no data on direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, or caregiving time, scoping itself to lost-labor cost only.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper ties disease stage to a steep per-patient cost difference, with disseminated/late disease costing far more per patient than early-stage disease despite being less common.

evidence.note: Per-patient cost for disseminated/late Lyme disease (5148 EUR, 2019) is reported as about 26.67 times the EM per-patient cost (193 EUR, 2019).

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper identifies a diagnostic-coding gap as a source of uncertainty in its hospital cost allocation.

evidence.note: The paper states there is no ICD-10-CM code for EM or PTLDS, so hospital costs were allocated to the broader disseminated/late category and coding quality could not be checked.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper quantifies a national population-level lost-labor cost estimate scaled from survey data to the full-time US workforce.

evidence.note: The paper scales a 2022 MEPS sample-based estimate to a national lost-labor cost of 12784168675.2 USD using BLS full-time worker counts.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper reports that the association between paid sick leave and having Long COVID did not reach statistical significance in its own analysis.

evidence.note: The paper reports an odds ratio of 0.9 (95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=0.51) for the paid-sick-leave/Long COVID association, below its own significance threshold.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper provides a breakdown of economic burden by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.
Neither paper provides a multi-year or lifetime cost projection; the Lyme disease paper is limited to a 6-12 month follow-up window and the Long COVID paper to a single 2022 calendar year.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers only - one Lyme disease paper reporting direct medical, non-medical, and productivity costs in 2019 euros, and one Long COVID paper reporting lost-labor/productivity costs in 2022 US dollars. Both papers present pooled national or population-level cost figures without demographic subgroup breakdowns, and both explicitly state that parts of total economic burden (such as long-term, caregiving, or direct medical costs) were left unmeasured. The two papers examine different cost categories, currencies, price years, and time windows, so their dollar figures cannot be added, divided, or otherwise combined into a single cross-condition number. Each paper also flags a different systemic gap specific to its own condition - a diagnostic-coding gap for Lyme disease and a lack of effective treatment for Long COVID. This is not a controlled study; it reflects only what these two independently built papers happen to report.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison covers two papers only - one Lyme disease paper (1 paper total, tagged for direct_costs, with all three limitations flagged as applying) and one Long COVID paper (1 paper total, tagged for employment, with two of the three limitations flagged as applying) - each built from a single uploaded document. This is a small, non-random sample reflecting whichever documents happened to be uploaded, not a controlled or representative comparison of either condition, and no paper in this sample covers both conditions.

learning_cards.headline: Lyme disease paper flags a fifth of medical costs unreimbursed
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports that 24.5% of direct medical costs (2019 euros) were not reimbursed by insurance.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not measure direct medical costs or insurance reimbursement at all, focusing only on lost-labor costs.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers add a measure of out-of-pocket or non-reimbursed direct medical costs to see whether a similar share goes unpaid by insurance?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID paper measures a lost-labor cost gap by infection status
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper finds a 1242.04 USD/person/year lost-labor cost gap for the Long COVID group versus people never infected, and a 478.91 USD/person/year gap versus people infected without Long COVID, scaling to 12784168675.2 USD nationally in 2022.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not measure lost-labor or employment-related costs at all, reporting only a direct medical cost share.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers estimate a comparable lost-labor cost gap between people with and without Lyme disease?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could prompt the Long COVID paper to look at non-reimbursed direct medical costs, while the Long COVID paper could prompt the Lyme disease paper to look at lost-labor costs, since each paper currently reports only its own category.
